title: Running a simulation
text:
This chapter describes how to launch a run — the scribe-mode I/O model, how to size it, and the run_schism_vm.sh launcher that wraps the whole workflow.


A run directory must contain a complete input set before launching:

Mesh & vertical grid: hgrid.gr3, hgrid.ll, vgrid.in
Initial conditions: elev.ic, salt.ic, temp.ic (+ tracer ICs)
Spatial flags / coefficients: the *.gr3 fields, fluxflag.prop, tvd.prop
Boundary forcing: bctides.in, *.th / elev2D.th.nc, TEM_*.th, AED_*.th
Atmospheric forcing: the sflux/ directory + sflux_inputs.txt
Rivers / point sources: source_sink.in, vsource.th, msource.th
Configuration: param.nml, aed.nml, and the aed/ parameter CSVs
Output dir: an outputs/ directory for SCHISM to write into

Each file is described in Directory & file structure.



SCHISM uses scribe-mode I/O: a subset of MPI ranks is reserved to write NetCDF output while the rest do computation. The integer after the binary name is NSCRIBE, the number of scribe ranks:
mpirun -np <NPROC> pschism_AED <NSCRIBE>

NPROC — total MPI ranks (compute + scribe)
NSCRIBE — ranks reserved for scribe-I/O
compute ranks = NPROC − NSCRIBE



As a rule of thumb, NSCRIBE ≈ the number of scribed-variable types (one per hydro/tracer variable) is a safe upper bound. Too low and the scribe ranks bottleneck; too high and compute capacity is wasted.



Total ranks
Reasonable NSCRIBE
Notes

4
small test runs

~one scribe per tracer


64
24–26
most ranks free for compute


144+

The Pioneer runs use NPROC = 64, NSCRIBE = 26 — the 26 reflects the scribed-variable count with the GEN_1 tracer adding one.




The Pioneer runs ship with run_schism_vm.sh, a no-SLURM wrapper that runs the model, checks the exit code, runs the combine step, and reports timings — all in one go. Run it from the run directory:
./run_schism_vm.sh
# or override any knob at invocation:
NPROC=32 NSCRIBE=8 ./run_schism_vm.sh

Run length and I/O cadence are set in param.nml — rnday (days), dt (timestep, s), nspool (output every N steps), and ihfskip (steps per output stack). The Pioneer runs use rnday = 91, dt = 45 s, 15-minute output spooled into daily stacks. See Run scenarios & log for the per-run settings.

title: Conservation Testing
text:
A budget is only as trustworthy as the conservation of the quantities that feed it. This chapter sets out the step-by-step checks we use to test and cross-check that a SCHISM-AED budget is accurate — what can go wrong, how to benchmark each term, and what we have learned from applying the checks to the Pioneer runs.
The checks below are implemented as diagnostic scripts in analytics/pioneer_region_flux/diagnostics/. They target a run by name via run_config.py, so the same check runs against 002 or 003 without editing paths:
python diagnostics/conservation_check.py --run 003 --days 14
active_run() resolves --run / --run-dir / SCHISM_RUN (default 002) and --days; the RunConfig derives all run-file paths, parses the start date from param.nml, and reads n_regions from fluxflag.prop.


Before trusting a budget it helps to know where conservation can break down in a coupled hydrodynamic–biogeochemical model. The recurring culprits are:

Source injection into small or dry cells. A point source adds volume and mass to its receiving element each step. If the injected volume is large relative to the cell volume — a high injection ratio \(\mathrm{rat}=Q\,\Delta t/\mathrm{bigv}\) — or the cell is intermittently dry, not all of the intended mass is retained.
Untracked boundary transport. flux.out only records transport across edges where adjacent fluxflag.prop values differ by exactly 1 (and neither is −1). Any control-volume perimeter that does not meet this rule is invisible to the boundary term.
Tidal cancellation. At a tidal gate the net transport is a small residual between large flood and ebb excursions, so sign and magnitude errors are easy to hide.
Coupling / numerical loss. In principle a tracer could be lost in the AED ↔︎ SCHISM hand-off or in transport; this must be ruled out before blaming the budget terms.

The remaining sections are the checks that isolate each of these.



Theory. A conservative tracer (no sources, sinks or reactions inside the domain) must be conserved exactly bar boundary exchange. Comparing a tracer carried by AED against one carried natively by SCHISM, with identical forcing, isolates whether any loss is in the AED coupling or in the shared transport.
What we find. TRC_tr1 (AED) and GEN_1 (SCHISM-native) are injected identically and evolve bit-for-bit together — so transport is conservative and the AED hand-off is not losing mass. This is the decisive first benchmark: it moves attention away from the biogeochemistry and onto the source and boundary terms.






Figure 1: Conservative-tracer benchmark: AED TRC_tr1 vs SCHISM-native GEN_1. Identical evolution rules out an AED coupling loss. Source: …/diagnostics/tr1_vs_gen1_compare.py






Theory. The boundary term (E) is read entirely from flux.out at the control-volume transect — for the Pioneer CV, the (3↔︎2) mouth gate. Its accuracy depends on (i) whether the flagged transect actually covers the whole perimeter, (ii) the sign/direction convention, and (iii) how the raw positive/negative components are combined.
What we find. Classifying every edge around the perimeter shows that a large part of the mouth is untracked — transport leaves through edges flux.out never sees.






Figure 2: Edge classification at the mouth: tracked (counted in flux.out) vs untracked perimeter edges. Source: …/diagnostics/mouth_edge_classification.py



Reconstructing the flux directly from model velocity × layer thickness on each mouth edge, and comparing against flux.out, recovers the missing transport — confirming the gap is a fluxflag coverage issue, not a model error, and checking the directionality of the reported sign.






Figure 3: Independent edge-flux reconstruction vs the flux.out transect. Source: …/diagnostics/edge_flux_reconstruction.py



Looking at the raw gate signal shows why care is needed: the net is a small residual between large, near-cancelling flood/ebb excursions. Separating the positive and negative components keeps that explicit.









Figure 4: Positive / negative / net breakdown at the (2↔︎3) gate. Source: …/diagnostics/check_flux_upwind.py











Figure 5: Raw cumulative flux.out components. Source: …/diagnostics/plot_flux_raw.py






This tidal cancellation is also why run 003 holds the tide flat for the first 14 days (the flat-tide method): with the excursions removed, the source term can be assessed on its own.



Theory. A point source should add exactly \(Q\,c\,\Delta t\) of tracer mass per step. Whether it does depends on the receiving cell: a high injection ratio rat or a dry/near-dry cell means the model cannot accommodate the full injection and mass is under-applied.
What we find. At the Pioneer River source the pulse drives a mean \(\mathrm{rat}\approx 7\) in a shallow, intermittently dry cell, implying only a fraction of the intended mass is retained per step — a genuine source-side loss, separate from the boundary issue above.






Figure 6: Source-cell diagnostics: dry fraction, column depth, injection ratio rat, and implied per-step retention. Source: …/diagnostics/src3_dry_rat_check.py






Theory. Source-cell problems are tied to the wider question of whether the upper river stays hydraulically connected. If the channel dries to disconnected pools over the tidal cycle, both the source injection and the transport of its load become unreliable.
What we find. The upper river is shallow and the wet channel narrows and widens with the tide, intermittently isolating the reach around the source — the context for the high rat above.






Figure 7: Upper-river bathymetry and wet/dry connectivity. Source: …/archive/upper_river_connectivity.py




Upper-river water depth over the tidal cycle (red = dry). Source: analytics/animations/upper_river_connectivity_animation.py.



Theory. The previous checks focus on conservative quantities; the final step is to account for every state variable over the region — cumulative source input, tracked transect flux, and control-volume vs domain-integrated mass — side by side, so reactive variables can be sanity-checked too.
What we find. per_variable_plots.py renders this three-panel account for all 20 variables. A few representative panels:









Figure 8: TRC_tr1











Figure 9: GEN_1











Figure 10: NIT_amm

Check

title: The budget framework
text:
This chapter describes the generic, region-agnostic mass-balance framework. The theory and tooling here apply to any control volume in any SCHISM-AED run; the Pioneer application follows in the next chapter.
The framework lives in analytics/nutrient_budget/. It is transferable — point it at any run and control volume; it has no hard-coded run paths.


Given a control volume (CV) — a set of mesh elements — and a tracer group (currently total nitrogen), the framework assembles a six-term budget:
\[
\frac{dM}{dt} = B + C + D + E + F + \text{residual}
\]








Term
Meaning
Source




A
storage \(M(t)\) and \(dM/dt\)
scribed state variables + layer height


B
internal sinks (denitrification + anammox)
3D rate diagnostics


C
atmospheric flux
*_atm sheet diagnostics


D
sediment–water interface flux
*_swi / *_dsf diagnostics


E
net boundary exchange
flux.out over fluxflag.prop regions


F
river point sources
vsource.th × msource.th



The residual is the closure error. In a well-posed budget it stays near zero; a systematic drift signals a missing or mis-signed term — which is exactly what the step-by-step checks in Conservation Testing are designed to catch.










Module
Role




budget.py
CLI entry point — runs the full six-term budget


tracer_groups.py
tracer-pool registry (the nitrogen bundle, signs)


geometry.py
hgrid I/O, element areas, NetCDF concat, node→element averaging


integrators.py
Terms A–D (storage, rates, surface fluxes)


boundary_fluxes.py
flux.out parser + Term E aggregator


point_sources.py
source_sink / vsource / msource → Term F


report.py
CSV / PNG / HTML writers


build_cv.py
define a CV from a polygon + fluxflag regions






python core/budget.py \
    --region       <region>.yaml \
    --tracer-group nitrogen \
    --outputs-dir  <run>/outputs \
    --hgrid        <run>/hgrid.gr3 \
    --param-nml    <run>/param.nml \
    --n-stacks     14 \
    --output-dir   ./_outputs/<name>
The --region YAML names the CV element list and the bounding fluxflag.prop regions; building one is covered in the next chapter.



Every run writes a self-contained set of outputs to its --output-dir:







Output
Contents




budget_timeseries.csv
every term, time-indexed


budget_stacked.png
instantaneous mass-balance, stacked area


budget_cumulative.png
cumulative time-integrals (tonnes N)


report.html
a narrated walk-through with the plots embedded, the closure check, and sanity notes



The report.html is the primary artefact to read — it bundles the plots, the closure residual, and commentary into one self-contained page. Rather than reproduce its content here, the Pioneer estuary chapter embeds and links a real example.



The diagnostic plots compare the observed storage change against the sum of the accounted-for terms. When the budget closes, the two track each other and the residual stays near zero; a growing residual points to a missing or mis-signed term. Volume and salinity are the cheapest checks, because they are conservative and well constrained — they are the first things to look at before trusting the nutrient terms.



Beyond the headline budget, the toolkit ships a set of diagnostic scripts that interrogate each term independently — the checks needed to trust (or distrust) a closure. They live in pioneer_region_flux/diagnostics/ and target a run by name (--run 002|003). In brief:

conservation checks — observed storage change vs source + boundary, per variable (conservation_check.py, global_balance.py);
conservative-tracer benchmarks — AED TRC vs SCHISM-native GEN (tr1_vs_gen1_compare.py);
transect assessments — independent edge-flux reconstruction and positive/negative/net breakdowns at the mouth (edge_flux_reconstruction.py, check_flux_upwind.py, mouth_edge_classification.py);
source & connectivity checks — injection-ratio and wet/dry diagnostics at the river source (src3_dry_rat_check.py, upper_river_connectivity.py);
per-variable accounts — a 20-variable gallery of source vs transect vs storage (per_variable_plots.py).

These are applied step by step in Conservation Testing.



The boundary term depends entirely on how the domain is partitioned into flux regions. fluxflag.prop labels every element with a region number, and SCHISM reports the tracer transport across the interface between regions of adjacent number into flux.out. These transects are the pre-configured “gates” through which a control volume exchanges mass with the rest of the domain.






Figure 1: The fluxflag.prop regions across the model domain — the pre-configured budget gates. Source: analytics/pioneer_region_flux/diagnostics/inspect_fluxflag.py



A control volume is then assembled from elements bounded by these regions. The Pioneer setup uses a simplified region set that makes the mouth (3↔︎2) transect explicit — defining such a region and reading its budget is the subject of the Pioneer Estuary chapter.

title: Mackay Regional Domain
text:
This chapter introduces the Mackay regional model — where it is and why it matters, the modelling approach, and the simulation scenarios maintained in this repository.


The model covers the Pioneer River estuary at Mackay, on the central Queensland coast of Australia, together with the adjacent coastal waters of the Coral Sea within the southern Great Barrier Reef lagoon. The Pioneer River drains a predominantly sugarcane catchment of roughly 1,500 km² and discharges through the city of Mackay to the sea.
Several features make this a demanding and interesting system to model:

Macro-tidal mouth. Mackay experiences one of the largest tidal ranges on the Australian east coast — spring ranges of around 6 m — so the estuary is strongly tide-dominated and the mouth exchanges large volumes each tide. (The boundary-forcing water levels span roughly 0.1–6.6 m, consistent with this range.)
Episodic, flood-driven freshwater. The climate is tropical with a pronounced summer wet season, and river flow is highly episodic — long dry spells punctuated by large floods. The most recent major event was the January 2023 Mackay flood, when the Pioneer River peaked near 2,600 m³ s⁻¹.
Catchment nutrient loads. The cane catchment delivers nutrient and sediment loads to a receiving environment adjacent to the Great Barrier Reef, so the estuary’s water quality and its exchange with the lagoon are a key management concern — and the motivation for coupling biogeochemistry to the hydrodynamics.

These characteristics — large tidal exchange at the mouth and sharp, flood-driven inputs at the river — are exactly the terms a nutrient budget must balance, and they shape the test scenarios described below.






Note



A location map of the model domain will be added here.





The model represents the Pioneer River estuary (Mackay, Queensland) and its adjacent coastal waters. The Pioneer River is the dominant freshwater input; it enters the model as a point source at the Bureau of Meteorology gauge 125013A (Dumbleton Pump Station) and drives the estuarine response during flow events.
The setup couples SCHISM hydrodynamics with AED biogeochemistry on a single unstructured mesh. River inflows enter as point sources (river forcing), the open ocean boundary is tidally forced (tidal forcing), the atmosphere is forced from gridded sflux fields, and biogeochemistry is configured through aed.nml. General conservative tracers (GEN) are included for mass-balance testing.



The repository tracks a sequence of runs under runs/, each building on the previous one. They are recorded in runs/RUN_LOG.md and described in full in the run log chapter.








ID
Name
Purpose




001
Pioneer_17
Original baseline setup (archived, not in this repo).


002
002_P18_flood
Pioneer 18 with an artificial flood pulse and a simplified fluxflag.prop to enable deep testing of the boundary-flux budget.


003
003_P18_flood_flat
Copy of 002 with the flood pulse and a quiescent (flat) ocean tide for the first 14 days, to isolate flux-direction inconsistencies across the Pioneer mouth.



Each run directory holds only the essential input/config files; outputs are regenerated and are not stored in the repository.



The flood pulse and the flat-tide variant exist to support a specific investigation: a nutrient mass balance over the estuary would not close, and the two candidate causes — mass loss at the high-rate river source, and untracked transport across the tidal mouth — were entangled. Run 003 holds the tide flat for two weeks so the source behaviour can be examined without tidal exchange, then restores the full tide. The budget work is the subject of Part 4.

title: Boundary & tidal forcing
text:
This chapter describes how the open ocean boundary is driven, and documents the flat-tide method used to build run 003.


The model has a single open ocean boundary. Its forcing is configured in bctides.in, which lists, per boundary and per variable, the type of forcing applied (elevation, velocity, temperature, salinity, and each tracer group). The flag line for the boundary reads, e.g.:
73 4 0 1 2 0 1   ! nodes, elevation, velocity, temperature, salinity, GEN, AED
Each integer is a forcing-type code. For elevation the relevant codes are:



iettype
Meaning
Input




1
uniform time history
elev.th


2
constant
value in bctides.in


3
tidal harmonics
amplitude/phase per node in bctides.in


4
space/time-varying
elev2D.th.nc


5
tidal + space/time
bctides.in + elev2D.th.nc






The flood run (002) uses iettype = 3: a pure tidal boundary built from eight constituents (M2, S2, N2, K2, K1, O1, P1, Q1), each with a per-node amplitude and phase. SCHISM reconstructs the boundary elevation as
\[
\eta(n,t)=\sum_k f_k\,A_{k,n}\,\cos\!\big(\omega_k t-\phi_{k,n}+(V_0+u)_k\big)
\]
where \(A_{k,n}\), \(\phi_{k,n}\) are the per-node amplitude and phase, and \(f_k\), \(\omega_k\), \((V_0+u)_k\) are the nodal factor, angular frequency and equilibrium argument from the header. The tide oscillates about 0 m (no \(Z_0\) term).



Run 003 holds the boundary flat (0 m) for the first 14 days, then restores the full 002 tide. A harmonic boundary is analytic for all time and cannot be “switched on”, so 003 instead uses iettype = 4 with a generated elev2D.th.nc file. That file reconstructs the same per-node harmonic as 002 but multiplies it by a time ramp:

days 0–14: \(\eta = 0\) at every boundary node (flat);
days 14–16: a cosine ramp of the tidal amplitude from 0 → 1;
days 16+: the full harmonic tide — identical to 002 from day 16 on.

The generator analytics/utilities/make_flat_tide_elev2D.py parses the constituents from 002’s bctides.in, writes the SCHISM elev2D.th.nc (dims time, nOpenBndNodes, nLevels=1, nComponents=1, one; ordered as bctides.in), and 003’s bctides.in is switched to iettype = 4 with the per-node harmonic blocks removed.






Note



Because the flat period is 0 m and the harmonic mean is also 0 m, the nramp_elev startup ramp in param.nml has no effect on the flat window and the post-ramp tide is unchanged — no param.nml edit is required.


This construction is what lets run 003 isolate the river-source behaviour from the tidal mouth exchange in the conservation testing.

title: Boundary & tidal forcing
text:
The flood run (002) uses iettype = 3: a pure tidal boundary built from eight constituents (M2, S2, N2, K2, K1, O1, P1, Q1), each with a per-node amplitude and phase. SCHISM reconstructs the boundary elevation as
\[
\eta(n,t)=\sum_k f_k\,A_{k,n}\,\cos\!\big(\omega_k t-\phi_{k,n}+(V_0+u)_k\big)
\]
where \(A_{k,n}\), \(\phi_{k,n}\) are the per-node amplitude and phase, and \(f_k\), \(\omega_k\), \((V_0+u)_k\) are the nodal factor, angular frequency and equilibrium argument from the header. The tide oscillates about 0 m (no \(Z_0\) term).

title: Boundary & tidal forcing
text:
Run 003 holds the boundary flat (0 m) for the first 14 days, then restores the full 002 tide. A harmonic boundary is analytic for all time and cannot be “switched on”, so 003 instead uses iettype = 4 with a generated elev2D.th.nc file. That file reconstructs the same per-node harmonic as 002 but multiplies it by a time ramp:

days 0–14: \(\eta = 0\) at every boundary node (flat);
days 14–16: a cosine ramp of the tidal amplitude from 0 → 1;
days 16+: the full harmonic tide — identical to 002 from day 16 on.

The generator analytics/utilities/make_flat_tide_elev2D.py parses the constituents from 002’s bctides.in, writes the SCHISM elev2D.th.nc (dims time, nOpenBndNodes, nLevels=1, nComponents=1, one; ordered as bctides.in), and 003’s bctides.in is switched to iettype = 4 with the per-node harmonic blocks removed.






Note



Because the flat period is 0 m and the harmonic mean is also 0 m, the nramp_elev startup ramp in param.nml has no effect on the flat window and the post-ramp tide is unchanged — no param.nml edit is required.


This construction is what lets run 003 isolate the river-source behaviour from the tidal mouth exchange in the conservation testing.

title: Pioneer Estuary
text:
This chapter applies the budget framework to the Pioneer estuary: how the control volume is defined, and what the nitrogen budget returns for the flood run.


A budget is computed over a control volume (CV) — a contiguous set of mesh elements whose seaward boundary coincides with the Pioneer Mouth flux transect and which is otherwise closed by land and the upstream river. For run 003 the CV is 16,344 elements (4.81 km²) and contains all three river point sources.






Figure 1: Pioneer estuary control volume (run 003): the selected CV cells (green fill) drawn on the model mesh, with the mouth fluxflag cells (flag-2 blue / flag-3 red outlines), the flag 2↔︎3 mouth transect (magenta), and the three river inflows (gold). Source: diagnostics/cv_definition_map.py.



How the CV is built — three steps, and the files to cross-check or remake it. (1) A polygon is drawn around the estuary in lon/lat and saved as cv_pioneer_estuary.csv; its seaward edge follows the Pioneer Mouth flag 2↔︎3 transect — the line where fluxflag.prop region-2 faces meet region-3 faces — so the CV boundary lands exactly on the flux-tracked gate. (2) build_cv.py reads the mesh (hgrid.gr3) and selects every element whose centroid falls inside the polygon (point-in-polygon), writing the 1-indexed element-ID list cv_pioneer_estuary_elements.txt — the exact array every budget script integrates over. (3) cv_definition_map.py overlays that element list on the mesh, the fluxflag.prop flags and the source_sink.in inflows (Figure 1) so the selection can be verified. To define a different CV, redraw the polygon CSV and re-run steps 2–3; the inputs are just hgrid.gr3, cv_pioneer_estuary.csv, fluxflag.prop and source_sink.in.


The region YAML names the CV element list and the bounding fluxflag.prop regions with their sign conventions (configs/pioneer_estuary.yaml):
name: pioneer_estuary
control_volume_elements: cv_pioneer_estuary_elements.txt
boundary_fluxes:
  - region_id: 3
    sign: +1
    label: "Pioneer Mouth (region 3 -> region 2): positive = bay -> estuary, INTO CV"
integrate_atm_over_cv: true
integrate_swi_over_cv: true



A critical subtlety for the boundary term: flux.out records transport only across mesh edges where the two adjacent fluxflag.prop values differ by exactly 1 and neither is −1. If part of the CV perimeter is the (−1, region) interface or a same-flag edge, transport through it is invisible to the budget. This turns out to be the heart of the Pioneer mouth problem.




Before quantifying the budget, it helps to see what is being budgeted. The conservative tracers injected at the river source spread through the estuary and exchange across the mouth transect — the storage and boundary terms the budget must capture. The dilute plume is clearest zoomed in on the Pioneer mouth:

Conservative-tracer plume around the Pioneer mouth (zoomed). Source: analytics/animations/animate_trc_zoomed.py.



Running the framework over this CV for the 14-day flood window produces the standard outputs. The stacked-area plot shows the instantaneous balance of terms; the cumulative plot integrates them to tonnes of nitrogen.









Figure 2: Instantaneous mass balance (stacked area). Source: nutrient_budget/core/report.py











Figure 3: Cumulative time-integrals (tonnes N). Source: nutrient_budget/core/report.py






The conservative checks come first. Volume and salinity should close tightly; if they do not, the nutrient terms cannot be trusted. The conservative tracers (GEN_1, TRC_tr1) give a second, source-driven check.









Figure 4: Volume and salinity closure. Source: …/diagnostics/conservation_check.py











Figure 5: Conservative-tracer closure (GEN_1, TRC_tr1). Source: …/diagnostics/conservation_check.py






A whole-domain balance infers the open-boundary term by difference, providing an independent view on closure:






Figure 6: Global mass balance — closing the ocean-boundary term by residual. Source: …/diagnostics/global_balance.py






Each run also writes a self-contained report.html — the plots, the closure residual, and the sanity commentary in one page. The report below is the 14-day nitrogen budget for run 002 (pioneer_N_002_14d):

Open the full report in a new tab →






Important



Read this budget with one caveat. Run 002 was produced on an earlier build affected by the “only NCS_ss1 registers” output bug, so its combined AED files contain only the sediment (NCS_ss1) diagnostics — none of the nitrogen rate, sediment–water or atmospheric diagnostics were saved. Terms B (internal sinks), C (atmospheric) and D (sediment–water) are therefore unavailable and set to zero, and the storage term uses a zCoordinates-derived layer thickness in place of ENV_layer_ht. The large residual consequently conflates those genuinely-missing terms with the conservation issues discussed next — it is not a pure closure error. A run on the fixed build that saves the full diagnostic set is needed for a closeable nitrogen budget.


For this run the residual does not close — the storage change far exceeds the tracked source and boundary terms. The forensic account of the conservation issues, and how an independent cross-check confirmed them, is the subject of Conservation Testing.

title: Building SCHISM-AED
text:
This chapter describes how to compile the coupled pschism_AED executable and the post-processing tools from source.
SCHISM-AED is built from the AED_Tools umbrella repository, which fetches the upstream SCHISM source, patches it with the AED-coupling glue, and compiles pschism_AED together with the SCHISM utilities — including combine_output11_MPI.






Tip



A condensed version of this build recipe (and the run/health-check steps in the next chapters) is kept alongside the file table in docs/quick-start/SCHISM_AED_file_table.md. This chapter is the fuller account.




On Ubuntu 22.04 (or similar):
sudo apt install libopenmpi-dev
sudo apt install libnetcdf-dev libnetcdff-dev
You also need git, make, gcc, gfortran (≥ 9, for modern Fortran / std=f2018), and CMake for the SCHISM core build.



# 1. Clone the umbrella repo
git clone https://github.com/AquaticEcoDynamics/AED_Tools
cd AED_Tools/

# 2. Pull the SCHISM source tree and all AED libraries
./fetch_sources.sh schism
./fetch_sources.sh all

# 3. Install runtime deps (see above) if not already present

# 4. Convenience symlink expected by the patch
ln -s schism a

# 5. Apply the AED-coupling patch to SCHISM
patch -p0 < schism-aed/aed-schism.xdiff

# 6. Graft AED into SCHISM's source tree
cd schism/src
ln -s ../../schism-aed/src/AED .
cd ../..

# 7. Compile
./build_schism.sh --with-aed

# 8. Confirm the executables landed
ls binaries/ubuntu/22.04/
Typical build time on a multi-core VM is 3–8 minutes.



build_schism.sh --with-aed produces:

pschism_AED_..._TVD-VL — the main model executable (the long suffix encodes the build options); often copied/symlinked to pschism_AED.
combine_output11_MPI — under schism/build/bin/, the post-process binary that assembles per-rank AED outputs.
combine_hotstart7 — combines per-rank hotstart files for restarts.

AED_Tools/
├── libaed-water/ libaed-benthic/ libaed-demo/ libaed-api/   AED libraries
├── schism/build/bin/
│   ├── pschism_AED_..._TVD-VL    the model executable
│   ├── combine_output11_MPI      the per-rank AED combiner
│   └── combine_hotstart7         hotstart combiner
└── binaries/ubuntu/<version>/    copies of the main executables






Note



The Pioneer runs use a GEN-enabled build (pschism_AED_GEN_BLD_STANDALONE_SH_MEM_COMM_TVD-VL) so that SCHISM-native general tracers are available — see AED & tracers.





build_schism.sh accepts flags for optional features. On a standard Ubuntu host with apt-provided OpenMPI + NetCDF, plain --with-aed is enough.







Flag
Effect




--with-aed
Compile and link AED (required for SCHISM-AED)


--need-netcdf_c / --need-netcdf_f
Build NetCDF-C / Fortran from source (if system version too old)


--need-openmpi / --need-mpich
Build the MPI stack from source


--all
Shorthand: extras + netcdf-c + netcdf-f + openmpi + gd



Run ./build_schism.sh --help for the full list.




Transient HYDRAULIC_STRUCTURES.mod copy error — a filesystem race in parallel make -j builds on network shares (Dropbox/CIFS/NFS). Just re-run the build; if it persists, make -j1 inside schism/build/ serialises and reveals the real error.
--need-netcdf-f typo warning — the flag uses an underscore (--need-netcdf_f); the dash form is a non-fatal warning.
MPI signature warnings (INTEGER(4)/REAL(8) from schism_msgp.F90 etc.) — upstream SCHISM warnings, harmless, not introduced by AED.
“Only NCS_ss1 registers” on a fresh AED run — a _FillValue type-check failure on stricter NetCDF/HDF5 stacks. See the SCHISM skill’s faq-and-gotchas.md for the fix.

title: Combining outputs & health checks
text:
This chapter covers the post-run assembly of the AED outputs and the quick sanity checks that confirm a run is healthy.


SCHISM writes two kinds of NetCDF output:

Scribed outputs (out2d_*.nc, salinity_*.nc, OXY_oxy_*.nc, …) are written by the scribe ranks directly onto the global mesh. They are ready to use — no combine needed.
AED diagnostic outputs are written per MPI rank as aed_data_<rank>_<stack>.nc. These must be reassembled onto the global mesh before analysis, producing aed_data_cmb_<stack>.nc.




cd outputs/
mpirun -np 4 combine_output11_MPI -b <BEGIN_STACK> -e <END_STACK> -o aed_data

-b 1 -e 14 combines stacks 1–14.
-o aed_data sets the prefix → produces aed_data_cmb_<S>.nc.

The combiner reads the local_to_global_<rank> partition maps written by SCHISM plus the per-rank aed_data_<rank>_<stack>.nc files for each stack in the range.



run_schism_vm.sh runs the combine automatically after a clean SCHISM exit, with conveniences:

COMBINE_END=auto discovers the highest stack number in outputs/, so the range never needs hand-editing as run length changes.
COMBINE_NPROC=auto resolves to min(NPROC, n_stacks).
COMBINE_ONLY=1 skips SCHISM and just combines whatever stacks exist — useful to salvage a prematurely killed run.
DELETE_PER_RANK_AFTER_COMBINE=1 (default) removes the per-rank aed_data_<rank>_<stack>.nc files once all expected cmb files exist — saving tens of GB per run. It verifies the combined files are present before deleting.




After a run, a cheap sanity sequence confirms it finished cleanly:
cd outputs
cat fatal.error            # should be empty (0 bytes = no fatal abort)
tail mirror.out            # should end with a clean finalization message
grep -i error nonfatal_*   # quick scan for rank-local warnings
ls aed_data_cmb_*.nc       # confirm combined files exist
run_schism_vm.sh performs these automatically and prints a summary, checking:

fatal.error is empty (non-empty ⇒ SCHISM aborted; its content names the failing rank and reason);
mirror.out exists and its tail shows a clean finalisation;
no nonfatal_<rank> files mention “error”;
the expected number of aed_data_cmb_*.nc files are present.

If mirror.out ends mid-step, note the last step number and check nonfatal_* and JCG.out (the pressure-solver convergence log) for clues.



To continue from a checkpoint:

Ensure the model wrote hotstart_<rank>_<stack>.nc (controlled by nhot_write in param.nml).
Combine them with combine_hotstart7 (also in schism/build/bin/).
Place the combined hotstart.nc in the run directory.
Set ihot = 1 (warm restart) or ihot = 2 (cold restart from hotstart) in param.nml, and re-launch as usual.

title: Pioneer SCHISM-AED Modelling Guide
text:
Welcome to the Pioneer SCHISM-AED Modelling Guide — a practical walkthrough of the Pioneer estuary coupled hydrodynamic–biogeochemical model and its analytics, intended to let a new user step through the model setup, run it, and analyse its outputs.






Note



This guide is in draft and under active development. Structure and content are subject to change.




The model resolves the tidal circulation of the Pioneer estuary on an unstructured mesh, coupled to a full biogeochemical state. The animation alongside shows the depth-averaged current speed over a spring–neap window — the flood and ebb pulses that drive exchange between the river, the estuary and the coastal ocean, and which the conservation tests in this guide must account for.
From this physical circulation the coupled model carries salinity, temperature, dissolved oxygen, nutrients and tracers — the basis for the analysis, animation and nutrient-budget workflows documented here.


Depth velocity magnitude over the model domain. Source: analytics/animations/animate_velocity.py.




The Pioneer model couples SCHISM (Semi-implicit Cross-scale Hydroscience Integrated System Model) — an unstructured-grid 3D hydrodynamic model — with AED (Aquatic EcoDynamics), a biogeochemistry library that adds tracer chemistry, dissolved oxygen, nutrient cycling and sediment processes. The combined pschism_AED executable solves physics and biogeochemistry in one MPI run.
This guide is organised into five parts:

Introduction — what the model is, key references, the Pioneer application, and how this repository is laid out.
Model Setup — every input file: mesh, vertical grid, boundary/tidal forcing, atmospheric and river forcing, AED configuration, and initial conditions.
Model Analysis — the output file structure, how to read the NetCDF outputs, and the animation toolkit.
Nutrient Budget — the control-volume mass-balance framework and the Pioneer-mouth flux investigation built on it.
Running the Model — building from source, running a simulation, combining outputs, and the record of run scenarios.




The parts are written to be read in order by a new user, but each chapter is self-contained enough to use as a reference. Code, file names, and paths are shown in monospace; chapters link to the actual scripts and configuration in the repository wherever possible.

quarto preview      # live dev server
quarto render       # full build → _output/
